events.title: Hopes new Bass Strait service will lead to cheaper shipping for farmers
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Tasmanian beef farmers to benefit from new Bass Strait shipping service direct to Victoria A new cattle and freight terminal in Victoria is expected to be operational by the end of October. ( ABC News ) Farmers on King and Flinders islands diversifying into live cattle markets interstate has led to a new freight and livestock terminal in Victoria's Gippsland region. The operator of Bass Strait Freight believes the new port will allow him to drop the cost price of cattle and general freight by about 50 per cent by bypassing mainland Tasmania. The new terminal at Port Anthony in South Gippsland is expected to open at the end of October. There will be a "big change" for cattle producers on Bass Strait islands when a new Victorian depot is complete that will allow shipping to bypass mainland Tasmania, a local freight service says. Bass Strait Freight operator David Harris says he is responding to farmer demand by developing a new service to a terminal at Port Anthony, in South Gippsland, that could take up to 40,000 cattle a year from King and Flinders islands. "We are taking all those cattle north and so the trend is there, we just have to respond to it. "We're quite optimistic that it'll be a make-or-break for our company and it'll be a big change for the way cattle are taken from the islands." The new service is expected to be cheaper for farmers by reducing reliance on Bass Strait Freight's home port at Bridport, in northern Tasmania, and the headaches that come with its shallow channel. The service direct to Port Anthony will take about 15 hours and is expected to be up and running by the end of October. The privately owned Victorian port at Corner Inlet is co-investing in the berth and livestock facilities along with Mr Harris. David Harris is co-investing in the new facilities. ( ABC News: Emily Smith ) Mr Harris has already been running services from King and Flinders islands to Port Welshpool, not far from Port Anthony, but he said it had its limitations. "That facility doesn't allow you to consolidate freight," he said. David Harris says the existing Victorian depot, Port Welshpool, has limitations. ( Supplied: David Harris ) Avoiding Bridport's shallow channel Bass Strait Freight has been pushing to secure a regular direct shipping route from King and Flinders islands to Victoria for some years. A ship often runs aground here. This operator is pushing for a fix David Harris's ship bottomed out with 400 cattle on board at the end of last year, leading to a 12-hour wait for the next high tide. He wants a solution. Its bid to reinstate port access at Apollo Bay, a service that existed for more than a decade until 2022, was unsuccessful. Sailing through Bridport's shallow channel has caused massive headaches for Mr Harris too. It is so shallow that most large boats have only a half-hour window either side of high tide to cross it. Bass Strait Freight has purchased two excavators to better maintain the channel, but Mr Harris admits it is not a permanent solution. "After 32 years of operations, with the sand building up outside the existing entrance, there won't be a regular shipping service from Bridport to Flinders Island if we can't get the channel realigned," he said. David Harris hopes the new terminal means he can avoid the Bridport channel, where his ship sometimes runs aground. ( King Island Ports ) Mr Harris said there was also potential to source cattle from northern Tasmania. Livestock and freight will travel on the modified Matthew Flinders IV, which will be permanently based at Port Anthony. He said this vessel was much more vulnerable to running aground when entering the harbour at Bridport. Farmers on King and Flinders islands produce roughly half of Tasmania's total cattle herd. Pricing and seasonal conditions dictate where those cattle end up each year. A number of beef producers on both islands have expanded their herds. One Flinders Island cattle farmer says the larger producers are increasingly "taking their stock north". ( ABC News: Laurissa Smith ) They are purchasing more land locally and some are finishing stock on farms and feedlots interstate. Mr Harris's plan to shift larger numbers of cattle from King and Flinders islands north, bypassing mainland Tasmania, has its detractors across the local beef industry. Fuel crisis driving some farmers to consider abandoning harvests When fuel is this high, there's an expensive aftertaste from putting food on your plate. But Flinders farmer Nick Campion believes the benefits will stack up in the long run.

events.title: Roadside stall operators question future of honesty box system after crimes
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Michelle Carter and her daughter sell homemade goods in the meat safe at the end of their driveway. ( Supplied: Michelle Carter ) Operators of a roadside pantry in SA's Murraylands have lost hundreds of dollars due to theft and vandalism. Roadside stall operators say they are dealing with more theft, prompting them to rethink the honesty payment system. Once the pantry in the Murraylands is fixed, it will be cemented into the ground and the money box reinforced. Roadside stalls are a much-loved tradition in regional and rural Australia, and the honesty payment system is a big part of the experience. But theft and vandalism is making some operators rethink the honour system. In South Australia's Murraylands, about 80 kilometres out of Adelaide, Michelle Carter and her family started selling goods at the end of their driveway in August. The pantry had been restocked shortly before the incident. ( Supplied: Michelle Carter ) Every Saturday morning, they restock the 100-year-old meat safe with everything from sauce and sourdough to cupcakes made by Ms Carter's 15-year-old daughter. But recently, when her kids went to put some freshly collected eggs into the pantry, they were met with a "heartbreaking" sight. "They found the pantry face down, the money box ripped off the side," Ms Carter said. She estimates about $60 in cash was stolen, along with about $300 worth of stock that was either taken or damaged. The incident occurred in broad daylight while the family was fencing in a nearby paddock. Most upsetting to Ms Carter was the damage done to the pantry, which the family had carefully restored. "If people are going to take stock and destroy that, then fine. But the pantry was expensive and we've spent a lot of time revamping it," she said. The pantry had been tipped over during the incident, breaking the glass jars inside. ( Supplied: Michelle Carter ) "There's only one place in South Australia that still make it[s parts], and that's in Port Pirie. So, we're in the process of trying to get some … so we can keep it original." For her 15-year-old daughter, the effort of baking fresh cupcakes on Friday night had gone to waste. "She was a little bit devastated, to be honest. I think she took it harder than me. She found it like a personal insult," Ms Carter said. "It's not even about finances … it's about the heartbreak of someone wanting to do that and ruin someone's effort and work that they put into doing something better for their lives," Ms Carter said. Once the pantry is restored, it will be cemented into the ground and the money box reinforced. Cameras have already been installed in preparation for the eventual reopening. Adelaide Barbaro gave up trying to sell flowers from her own roadside stall after just three months following a series of thefts of both product and money. Adelaide Barbaro now sells flowers direct to florists. ( Supplied: Adelaide Barbaro ) Located in One Tree Hill, on the outskirts on Adelaide, Ms Barbaro decided to sell directly to florists instead. "It's quite sad because I love the idea of roadside stalls and being able to do that little thing from home," she said. "You'd have that initial excitement of a few sales, and then ultimately those bad experiences just, it wasn't a good feeling. "My kids would see how much effort I was putting in, and it would be Saturday morning, Sunday morning, making these bouquets when that should be really family time." Though it was ultimately not the right business model for her, Ms Barbaro said she did not regret starting out with a roadside stall. "I think it can really work for some people … the experience is 99 per cent joyful and honest," Ms Barbaro said. "You've just got to work out what works for you, I suppose." Ms Barbaro ran her roadside stall for about three months. ( Supplied: Adelaide Barbaro ) Ms Carter believes the honesty payment system still has a place, but her experience has made her more reserved about it. "You'll have some losses in a business all the time from theft, even in big shops," she said. "But as for the money side of it, I'm not sure that money belongs up at the end of someone's driveway anymore." Though cash will still be an option for now at the 90 Acre Pantry, if there was another theft Ms Carter said she would move to only accepting online payments. "If someone was hungry and they took a jar of relish, well, I'm not going to punish them. But if someone wants to steal all our money, then that's maybe a different story," she said. After finding the damage, Ms Carter initially planned to close down the roadside pantry.

events.title: Mark Zuckerberg predicts Muse will become a "personal superintelligence" for billions.
events.summary: Meta on Wednesday debuted "Muse Charm," a new, keychain-sized AI handheld device it will use to bring its viral Muse assistant to the masses. Why it matters: Meta has raced ahead of OpenAI , Apple and other companies that are working on a new crop of small AI devices, revving up the massive interest Muse has generated in the market. "We've packed a lot of technology in this little guy," Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg said at the event. "So if you're not wearing glasses, this is going to be by far the fastest way to talk to your Muse and to show them what's going on around you." Driving the news: The Muse Charm will be available for purchase by December, and the company is the first tech giant to unveil its plans for an entirely new category of device. OpenAI has spent billions to build a hardware division, so Meta's advance on the category is likely to stun many analysts and investors. Meta has also poured billions into hardware, most notably VR, an effort that most analysts have written off as a waste. Zuckerberg has long held that a convergence of those investments with AI could make that bet pay off. Catch up quick : In addition to Charm, Meta announced new Muse capabilities including live video chat, real-time voice conversations with custom voice options and an e-mail address for each person's agent. Meta announced new retail partners, including Walmart, Best Buy, Gap, Sephora, Wayfair and more, a growing list that makes Amazon's decision not to allow Muse stand out. Muse has prompted a stock selloff in recent days as investors fear an end to stickiness between brands and customers. Meta said Muse is coming soon to its AI glasses, though it declined to be more specific than "in the coming months." "I expect that Muse is going to grow into the personal superintelligence that billions of people around the world are going to use to accomplish their goals and improve their lives," Zuckerberg said during his Meta Connect keynote on Wednesday. Beyond Muse, Meta used the event to debut a range of new hardware along with new privacy options that could make the gear more palatable to the mainstream. Meta's first audio-only glasses aim to appeal to those who want the benefit of open-air sound and an always available AI assistant without the cost and potential creepiness that comes from the camera-equipped version. The new models, which will be available later in October, start at $349. Meta is also updating its Ray-Ban and Meta Glasses lines with modest improvements and new designs. The more radical shift is coming on the VR side of things , and Meta previewed a much slimmer, $1,299 headset due out next spring. The big picture: Meta has invested heavily in glasses and AI over the last several years. Now it sees those giant bets converging. "It just feels really clear that [AI]'s what's going to enable the next big platform," said Alex Himel, Meta's vice president of wearables. "You're really starting to see that vision of VR and AR converging into glasses, starting to happen sooner." Between the lines: Meta is continuing a big shift on the privacy front. The company had already said it is working on a confidential virtual machine option for the Muse assistant. On Wednesday, Meta added that it is also readying "Private Processing" for AI glasses, a system designed to keep data protected even while it is being processed in the cloud, similar to Apple's Private Cloud Compute.

events.title: OpenAI agents ‘infiltrated Australian government website’
events.summary: Australia’s Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has revealed an OpenAI agent “infiltrated an Australian government website” while trying to research medical statistics. Albanese said the incident occurred in June and involved an agent gaining unauthorized access to a portal that stores statistics related to Medicare, Australia’s national health insurance scheme. “The AI agent accessed both public and non-public files,” the PM said, before describing the portal as holding “non-sensitive Medicare information relating to data and statistics such as spending.” Australia’s Signals Directorate, a signals intelligence and cybersecurity agency, is investigating the incident. Albanese said the government currently believes none of its other systems were compromised, and that OpenAI’s agents did not access personal information. The PM described the situation as “obviously unacceptable” and said he spoke with OpenAI CEO Sam Altman – who is also attending the UN meetings – “to express Australia's extreme concern about this incident.” Albanese also “expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred. The nature of the way that that notification occurred as well was unacceptable.” OpenAI told The Register it discovered the incident during the review of “misaligned behavior” it disclosed last week, and which led it to report six occasions on which its agents behaved unexpectedly and/or dangerously. “During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation,” an OpenAI spokesperson told The Register by email. “In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend.” “The information accessed included aggregate health statistics and internal file names,” the spokesperson added. OpenAI say the incident occurred in June, and that it notified Australia’s government on September 10. “During that time, we were validating and investigating the facts and what information had been accessed,” the spokesperson told The Register. We’ve asked OpenAI for more information about the incident, incuding whether this mess was one of the six examples of misaligment it revealed last week, and will update this story if we receive a substantial response. It is unclear why Albanese waited two weeks to disclose the incident, but ahead of the UN meeting Australia signed the Call for Control of Frontier AI Models, a 21-nation proposal for AI regulation. The PM is also using his visit to the UN to launch a bid for Australia to win a non-permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council. Australia last year used the UN meeting to promote its ban on children under 16 accessing social media. Albanese is widely expected to discuss his government’s proposed digital duty of care for tech platforms, which would require tech companies to avoid foreseeable harm to users, at this year’s meetings. The PM sees taking on Big Tech with strong regulations as a political winner, often linking the government’s actions to reducing the likelihood that children will self-harm. He often uses the phrase “we need to shape technology rather than allow it to shape us” to summarize his government’s policy. Every Australian has a Medicare account, the scheme is popular, and is a signature policy of Albanese’s Labor Party. OpenAI’s actions therefore give the PM a weapon to wield as he advocates for stronger regulation of tech companies. Albanese is trying to enact those regulations without scaring away investment. He had a win last week when Anthropic decided to become a long-term tenant of a 1.4GW datacenter cluster currently under construction down under. The PM faces criticism, however, over hints that in order to attract investment he may water down Australian copyright laws. Australia does not have the fair use exemptions that AI companies relied on to scrape content in other jurisdictions. Albanese has said any changes to copyright laws will embody two principles: creators “will have control over their intellectual property” and “any use needs to be monetized,” but hasn’t offered details on what that will mean. APRA AMCOS, an organization that represents Australian composers and musicians, last week criticized AI companies’ approach to gathering training data. "They have found the money for nearly every lobbying firm in Canberra. They have found the money for datacenters, power and Nvidia chips,” wrote CEO Dean Ormston. “But they have no intention of paying for the single most important ingredient in training and running a frontier large language model, which is creative content. And it isn't only Australia's IP they want. It's Australia and the world's IP, trained on in datacenters here without a single license agreement." ® UPDATED AT 2:15 AM UTC SEPTEMBER 24 to add news that OpenAI advised Australia's government of the incident by using the relevant agency's generic publicdisclosures@ email address rather than approaching government officials. That decision drew further criticism from Australian lawmakers. Prime Minister Albanese has also informed two of Australia's State goverments that OpenAI's agents also attacked their sites - a crime agency and a health department.

events.title: Trump to Venezuela's Rodriguez: Elections need to happen
events.summary: In his first-ever meeting with Venezuela's new leader, President Trump emphasized the need to keep oil flowing, relations warm and that country's elections on the horizon, White House sources tell Axios. Why it matters: Trump did not insist on a future election date in his meeting with Venezuela's acting president Delcy Rodriguez , but he emphasized their importance as a crucial final step in Venezuela's evolution into a full-fledged democracy, the sources said. "You have to have elections at the end of the day," Trump said to Rodriguez at one point, one of the sources briefed on the meeting said. Zoom in: Trump held the roughly 15-minute meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York to thank Rodriguez for their good working relationship after the U.S. ousted her one-time socialist ally, Nicolas Maduro, on Jan. 3. Since then, the Trump administration has struck oil and gold-mining deals with Venezuela, which had been a U.S. adversary for more than a quarter-century. Venezuela has one of the world's largest sovereign debt problems of $300 billion — larger than its gross domestic product — which needs to be restructured before the country holds elections, U.S. officials say. "The country can't succeed until that is solved," a White House official said. What they're saying: "We held a historic meeting with the president of the United States, Donald Trump, with whom we discussed strengthening the bilateral relationship between our countries and advancing a cooperation agenda in strategic areas such as energy, mining, and security," Rodriguez posted Tuesday night on X. The post included a photo of Rodriguez holding up two fingers in a "V" (for Venezuela) and Trump giving his characteristic thumbs-up. Friction point: The photo outraged the small but vocal Venezuelan diaspora community in the U.S., where critics want to hear more about Venezuela elections and less about deals. On the same day Trump and Rodriguez met, allies of Venezuela opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize Laureate Marina Corina Machado went public to complain that she has been blocked from re-entering the country. In the Miami area, home to both Secretary of State Marco Rubio and a sizable population of Venezuelan exiles and expats, former Democratic Senate candidate and Rep. Debbie Mucarsel Powell, posted the image on X and urged people to register to vote. "Tell every single member of the South Florida delegation that you are done with the lies and the blatant corruption. No Mas!" she wrote . Between the lines: The U.S. wants Venezuela's elections to be called by Venezuelans via the country's new National Reconciliation Council, which represents various political parties in the country. It's a three-step plan: Change the composition of the Venezuelan Supreme Court to make it more representative of the country. The opposition is going to get to nominate justices, an official said. Reform the National Electoral Commission to ensure there's not a repeat of 2024, when it manipulated the vote count and stole the election from Edmundo González on Maduro's behalf. Announce an election date. Trump, however, pointedly did not say when he wants that to be. Inside the room : Trump and Rodriguez were joined by two Venezuelan officials as well as Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles and White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller. Trump did most of the talking and also regaled Rodriguez with a description of the precision U.S. military operation that ousted Maduro. "It was warm. It was friendly. But it was also direct," one of the sources said about Trump's discussion of the importance of future elections. "She acknowledged it. She said she wants elections too," the source said. Zoom out: The multiple challenges Venezuela is facing from the legacy of socialist mismanagement to the earthquakes that damaged the country this summer make calling an election date even more complicated, U.S. officials say. "We don't want to have an election, have a democratically elected government take over and inherit an economic catastrophe within six months," said one. "A democratic government is going to be facing massive street protests over inflation, the economy. It could threaten the entire thing." The intrigue : By process of elimination, insiders say a Venezuelan election in the summer or fall of 2028 makes more sense because it would give the country more time to repair its finances and electoral system. Trump also would like to leave office with the legacy of removing a dictator, fixing a country and fostering democracy — but he might want to wait until the final months in office so the U.S. could still exert outsized influence on Rodriguez's government. Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) has called for Venezuela to hold elections on July 24, 2027, but Trump administration officials and allies say that might be too early. "If it can be in '27, that would be great. We would like that," an official said, cautioning that Venezuelans need to lead and need to fix their debt problem first. "Whether the date for those conditions to be met are 2027 versus 2028 is still up in the air," the official said. "It certainly can't go on indefinitely."

events.title: SoftBank-backed Carro said to mull first dual Nasdaq-SGX IPO
events.summary: Carro has filed confidentially for an initial public offering in the US and recently submitted paperwork for a Singapore listing as well, people familiar with the matter said. Carro, a SoftBank-backed used-car marketplace, is considering a dual IPO listing on Nasdaq and Singapore Exchange's Global Listing Board, potentially raising $400-500 million. The dual-listing system allows companies to list simultaneously in the US and Singapore with a single set of documents, aiming to boost Singapore's market liquidity and company base. Singapore's IPO market shows growth but remains small compared to Hong Kong and India; initiatives include substantial fund allocations to support local stock investments. NEW YORK – Used-car marketplace Carro is considering offering shares on the Singapore Exchange’s Global Listing Board, people familiar with the matter said, potentially positioning it to be the first company to use the new dual-listing mechanism with Nasdaq Inc. Carro has filed confidentially for an initial public offering in the US and recently submitted paperwork for a Singapore listing as well, according to the people, who asked not to be identified because the information is not public. The Singapore-based company, which is backed by SoftBank Group, could raise as much as US$400 million (S$510 million) to US$500 million, the people said. It is targeting a dual listing later in 2026 or in the first half of 2027, the people said. Deliberations are ongoing and details of the potential offering could change, according to the people. Carro could also decide against a Singapore listing depending on investor demand, they added. “The company considers and evaluates potential financing needs and opportunities from time to time and will make disclosures when appropriate to do so,” a spokesperson for Carro said in an e-mailed statement. Carro’s move is a boon for Singapore as it seeks to improve liquidity and broaden its base of publicly traded companies. Under the dual-listing system , which was first announced in 2025, companies need only prepare a single set of documents to float simultaneously in the US and Singapore, and the timing of their debuts will be aligned. Requirements include having at least S$2 billion in market value. DayOne Data Centers had also previously been considering a listing on SGX’s Global Listing Board that could have made it the first to use the new mechanism. The company has since decided not to pursue a concurrent dual listing and will instead focus on its US IPO for now, according to people familiar with the situation. DayOne confidentially filed for a US IPO in August and could raise US$5 billion, Bloomberg News has reported. It may still look to list in Singapore later, the people said. A representative for DayOne declined to comment. Singapore has not hosted a listing of US$1 billion or more since 2018, when South Korean internet company Kakao Corp. sold global depositary shares, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. IPOs in the city-state have fetched about US$1.1 billion in 2026 so far, a 33 per cent increase from the same period in 2025. While that is an improvement, largely thanks to UI Boustead REIT’s offering, it is a fraction of the proceeds in Hong Kong, which amounted to about US$48 billion, and India, which raised about US$11 billion. In other market initiatives, Singapore also set aside an initial S$5 billion in 2025 to be allocated to selected fund managers to invest in local stocks. In February 2026, it topped that up with another S$1.5 billion. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Meta is trying VR glasses (again), this time with more IMAX
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Disrupt ticket savings of up to $200 + 50% off a second ends Sept 25, 11:59 p.m. PT. REGISTER HERE. Meta is renewing its quest to make virtual reality a thing. At its Connect event on Wednesday, the company announced Meta VR Glasses, its newest entry into the VR market, which will be available next spring starting at $1,299.99. These glasses actually seem quite promising, thanks to a substantially lighter form factor and a host of new entertainment integrations — including (allegedly) IMAX compatibility. Moments before unveiling them, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg reminded the audience that the company had decided awhile ago to shift its focus away from the Metaverse and build fewer VR devices until it had real breakthroughs. “This is a breakthrough,” he exclaimed before showing off the glasses. “A lot of people agree that augmented reality glasses with holograms are clearly going to be part of the future, but we’ve also heard that a lot of people are less interested in wearing a headset. So we have built a new kind of VR device that delivers the same magical feeling of presence and immersion with high-resolution displays and views of the world around you in a form factor that is a pair of glasses for the first time.” Meta says that the glasses are five times lighter than the Meta Quest 3 — and they look much more like normal eyewear than the bulky headsets the company has released before. The frames are made of magnesium alloy, and the glasses are powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Reality Elite processor. They connect to a computing puck that doubles as a battery, which users can just slip into their pocket to use the glasses on the go. The glasses are largely built for entertainment. Micro-OLED panels built into the lenses provide what Meta calls a 5K Infinite Display with 37 pixels per degree, along with Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos audio support. Users will be able to download and watch movies. Perhaps one of the more unique features of the glasses, however, is that Meta is pitching them as a great way to enjoy IMAX-captured films. Indeed, the company calls the glasses the “first IMAX-enhanced certified VR device ever” and says they will be one of the few ways to experience the expanded aspect ratio that defines IMAX’s distinct high-resolution viewing experience. The glasses also support 3D content, including movies that integrate a user’s physical space into their viewing experience. Meta says that it has teamed up with Disney and that in November, Disney+ users will be able to stream specific movies — including certain Marvel movies — in 3D. Meta says that users will be able to watch specific movies and have their surroundings “transformed with immersive environments, dynamic effects, stunning 3D visuals, and spatial audio” — essentially converting the movie into a VR gaming-type experience. The glasses will also come with Meta AI — its automated virtual assistant — built in, which means that users will be able to talk to the glasses and automate various tasks via voice command. For instance, Meta says you’ll be able to start a movie just by asking your glasses to do so. Other ways to issue commands include hand gestures. events.title: Hands-on with Meta's next VR headset
events.summary: Meta's new virtual reality glasses take a big step toward being something an average person might be willing to wear, ditching much of the bulk as well as the need for handheld controllers. Why it matters: Unlike Meta's Ray-Bans, its VR devices have struggled to break out of their gamer niche and into the mainstream. Yes, but: In order to slim them down, the new Meta VR Glasses require a wired "puck" that can be held or clipped onto a belt. It contains much of the device's computing horsepower, including its processor, battery and storage. Zoom in: I spent about half an hour on Tuesday using a prototype of the new specs, which are controlled through a combination of eye-tracking, hand gestures and voice commands. Magnetic prescription inserts attach easily, similar to the approach Apple took with Vision Pro. Zoom out: The glasses are designed to serve a range of purposes from watching a movie or immersive concert to playing games and getting work done. I played a reimagined version of Beat Saber that cleverly remaps the music game for control via hand motions. I watched a clip from last year's NBA Finals. I used a trio of virtual monitors to do some "vibe coding" on a website, with one display showing the Muse terminal and another previewing the site itself. Meta sees these VR glasses as a "general device," Meta VP of product Angela Chang told Axios. "It's not built for any specific use case per se." My thought bubble: It's the most practical combination I've seen of an Apple Vision Pro-class device in a headset I'd be willing to wear outside of the house. The big picture: Google is working on a similar device, known as Project Aura, set to debut later this year and built in partnership with Xreal. Meta touts its wider field of view and higher optical quality, among other advantages over Aura. Between the lines: As for why it won't arrive until next spring, Meta executives say they want to be sure it makes a good first impression, especially inside a VR ecosystem. "We really are trying to strive for a very high bar on the software quality and experience side," Chang said. The bottom line: Meta said it has modest expectations for unit sales, but success will look like attracting folks beyond gamers, Chang said. "Are we bringing in new people into VR who, you know, maybe in the past would have looked at the Quest and said, 'Nah, that's not for me?'"

events.title: Meta introduces camera-free AI glasses
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Disrupt ticket savings of up to $200 + 50% off a second ends Sept 25, 11:59 p.m. PT. REGISTER HERE. Confirming earlier reports , Meta announced its first pair of camera-free AI glasses, the clunkily named Ray-Ban Meta Audio, at its Connect 2026 conference on Wednesday. Designed to combat criticism around the more malicious use cases for AI glasses, which saw them nicknamed “pervert glasses” by some, the new devices will be audio-only, offering the ability to listen to music and podcasts, take calls, translate speech, and communicate with Meta’s AI assistant, Muse. The glasses are designed by Meta’s partner in its AI hardware efforts, EssilorLuxottica, and will start at $349. While Meta today offers a range of AI glasses in a variety of styles, colors, and capabilities, the audio-only glasses could help the brand recover from some of the reputational damage after critics pointed out how people , often men , were using AI glasses to record videos without subjects’ consent. Meta attempted to mitigate this issue with an update that would disable the camera if the LED light that indicated the glasses were recording was ever tampered with. However, the creepiness factor remained. This latest device could prove to be more popular for that reason, while also providing an answer to something like Apple’s Siri-powered AirPods. “Once you get used to high-quality audio, it’s just a thing that you want all the time, right?” Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said during a keynote Wednesday, adding that the company after working on the idea realized it could design a whole new category of glasses around audio glasses. Because they don’t have to house cameras, the glasses are slimmer than Meta’s other models and weigh only 43 grams. They also have adjustable temple tips, swappable nose pads, overextension hinges, and battery life of up to 12 hours on a single charge, Meta claims. With the included charging case, that battery life extends to up to 48 hours. They’ll also come in a variety of colors and options — 23 color and lens combinations in total — and in two new styles, a retro-inspired “Clubmaster” Ray-Ban style and “Burbank,” described as more of a “classic, timeless, rectangle shape.” Like other Meta glasses, you can order them with your optical prescription as well, if needed. The glasses will be available for preorder on October 13, the company noted. Alongside the glasses, Meta announced its next-generation AI glasses (the ones with cameras), the Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 3). In addition to the Ray-Ban Meta Wayfarer, there will also be two new styles, the Aviator and Zena — the latter offering more of a cat-eye frame shape. These will have a 12 MP camera that supports 3K Ultra HD video, a six-mic array, and up to nine hours of battery life. The glasses Meta launched with EssilorLuxottica will also see an expanded lineup of styles and colors as well as a new partnership with singer Lisa, which follows the company’s earlier brand partnership with Kylie Jenner. The glasses will also roll out to more countries globally, Meta said. All of Meta’s AI glasses will, of course, feature access to its newer personal AI assistant, Muse. The company also teased other coming updates, including support for Dolby Atmos Capture, a feature that picks the best photo from multiple frames, an option to choose landscape or portrait modes, hearing enhancements for those with hearing loss, more detailed responses, different audio modes, customizable controls, and something called “private processing” that Meta claims will prevent the company from seeing your data. events.title: Qld council says costs prevent it hitting recycling targets
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Rockhampton Council warns escalating costs prevent it hitting recycling targets Topic: Recycling and Waste Management Tony Williams is calling on the Queensland government to help cover the costs of transporting recyclables for processing. ( Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council ) The Rockhampton Regional Council is calling on the state government for a subsidy to help cover the growing cost of transporting recyclables to the south-east corner for processing. Mayor Tony Williams says the council cannot achieve state-imposed recycling targets as it struggles to attract another company to develop a materials recovery facility locally. The Queensland government is designing a new fund to be spent on helping regional councils send recycling for processing. A regional Queensland council is warning it cannot meet state-imposed recycling targets with the growing cost of moving materials hundreds of kilometres for processing. Each year 10,000 tonnes of household recyclables collected from the Rockhampton region are driven 600 kilometres to a facility on the Sunshine Coast. Waste services cost the local council $3 million per year with more than one-third of that bill going to transportation fees. In June, the Queensland government released its waste strategy and set an overall recycling target of 65 per cent by 2035 , with major regional communities including Rockhampton expected to halve the amount of waste it sent to landfill. The Queensland government has set an overall recycling target of 65 per cent by 2035. ( ABC News: Ellie Willcox ) Rockhampton Mayor Tony Williams said his council was struggling to improve recycling rates, especially as fuel prices soared. "We've done our waste plans and [our staff] are saying that we can't achieve the targets that the state government is putting onto councils," he said. Recyclables from central Queensland households were previously processed at a private materials recovery facility in Rockhampton. But that was destroyed by a battery fire in 2020. The council has so far been unable to attract private companies to develop a similar facility. The council has been unable to find a firm to develop a materials recovery facility locally. ( ABC Radio Canberra: Jolene Laverty ) Mayor Williams said the local government spent about $300 per tonne to send its recyclables for processing, compared to about $100 a tonne for councils in south-east Queensland. "The cookie-cutter approach to increasing recycling really doesn't help when the tyrannies of distance and the cost to transport that material is ever-increasing," he said. "With the state government wishing to increase recycling locally, there's no real [financial] benefit unless we get some subsidies towards those transport costs." In a statement, state environment minister Andrew Powell said the government was providing support for recycling in regional areas, with $11 million in new funding for infrastructure. The government was also designing a new fund to be spent on helping regional councils send recycling for processing. The state government is hoping a new fund can help regional councils send recycling for processing. ( ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale ) Australian Council of Recycling chief Suzanne Toumbourou said the federal government should never have shelved national packaging reforms , which would have eased the burden on regional communities. "It's extraordinarily disappointing to see that lack of progress in packaging reform," Ms Toumbourou said. "We should have had regulatory certainty about the fact that burden would be shared much better across the supply chain and much more responsibility would be placed on producers." In a statement, federal environment minister Murray Watt said the government's focus was to work with state and territory governments to reduce waste by harmonising packaging and recycling policy in Australia.

events.title: Vogue sent robots down the runway at Vogue World, and people were not impressed
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Disrupt ticket savings of up to $200 + 50% off a second ends Sept 25, 11:59 p.m. PT. REGISTER HERE. Vogue World closed its Milan edition this week with a troupe of robots — perhaps a preview of what’s coming when the event descends on San Francisco next year. Vogue World is the magazine’s annual traveling spectacle, now in its fifth year: part runway show, part celebrity showcase, part variety hour, part ad-sales opportunity , staged in a different city each time. It has run through New York, London, Paris, and Hollywood. This year’s Milan edition was marketed as a tribute to Italian craftsmanship and “the human touch” in an age of technology, which makes what happened next a little strange. During the act titled The Age of Intelligence, humanoid robots made by the Chinese firm Unitree walked into the Galleria to Gigi D’Agostino’s “L’Amour Toujours.” They waved their arms in the air, imploring onlookers to clap. One did a lasso. They were not wearing clothes. The pained expression of Alessandro Michele, the creative director of Valentino, quickly went viral. Vogue World Milano ends (appropriately Europoor-kitschily) with tiny robottini dancing to L’Amour Toujours while Alessandro Michele slowly dies inside pic.twitter.com/xicYWWl6VW I haven’t seen a single thing about the actual fashion that was presented at Vogue World Milan. Instead, everyone is talking about the robots. (These same robots have been making headlines worldwide for their dance moves , and for falling and breaking .) Similar robots turned up on the runway at London Fashion Week, which is happening now. Vogue turned heads earlier this year when it announced that the next edition will be in San Francisco, arguably one of the least stylish cities in the United States. The timing isn’t coincidental. Anna Wintour has aligned herself ever more closely with the tech barons of our time, and Vogue World Milan was itself sponsored in part by Meta Glasses, with additional support from OpenAI. It was one of those moments that reveals how thoroughly tech exists in a bubble, and that not everyone is happy with the rapid adoption of new technology, or by Vogue cozying up to the symbols of the insanely rich — and only getting richer — tech titans during a cost-of-living crisis. That’s before you get to AI, mass surveillance, the displacement of labor, and the energy crisis, all of them overseen by the same titans. For some, a robot on a runway is further proof of what is going wrong in the world right now. miuccia prada when the fuckass robot walked out during vogue world pic.twitter.com/SebwpV0zkl We are all Alessandro Michele, sitting front row at Vogue World Milan, having an existential crisis about the absolute state of things while robots awkwardly dance about. Numb to the pain at this point. Madness. just got off the phone with the creative director of Vogue World. First question he asked me. “So you hated the robots?” 🤭 Full interview on Substack tomorrow 👀 https://t.co/FTa3gumPgY — Louis Pisano (@LouisPisano) September 23, 2026 “I’m annoyed by the celebrities cheering the whole thing,” one tech founder wrote me on Instagram. “It’s sick and gloom. People are literally losing jobs and livelihoods because of these things. They need to stop encouraging it. What’s it even modeling? Headphones?” One fashion reporter friend simply said “No,” when I asked for thoughts on the robots and Vogue World San Francisco. Jason Johnson, founder of Culture Impact Agency, noted that Vogue has been trying to build a relationship with Silicon Valley for at least the past decade, highlighting when Jony Ive co-hosted the Met Gala back in 2015. The dancing robots at Vogue World Milan were inevitable, then, as is Vogue World San Francisco and as was Jeff Bezos and his wife, Lauren Sanchez, getting the splashy Vogue wedding cover and co-hosting the 2026 Met Gala. “Publications are figuring out new ways to make money and tech has money,” he told me. “Vogue has the cultural influence and access that those tech people want.” Both sides win in the end, he said. Still, something about the way Vogue is going about this feels unnatural. Muna Ikedionwu, founder of MKEDI, a strategy firm for early-stage startups, said what she found most interesting about the robots is that they don’t fully represent the innovation and progress that’s actually happening in the creative technologist space. “I’ve seen such incredible examples of engineering and AI being used to influence fashion, being used to influence design and art,” she told me, adding that robots walking down the runway doesn’t even scratch the surface of what is happening right now at the intersection of fashion and tech. She points to the artist duo AA Murakami , who created Olympian Eileen Gu’s dress of bubbles at this year’s Met Gala .

events.title: Exclusive: Thune plans another leader bid as Senate GOP fights to survive
events.summary: Senate Majority Leader John Thune plans to run for another term as GOP leader, even if Republicans lose the chamber's majority, he told Axios in an exclusive interview Wednesday in his Capitol office. Why it matters: Thune (R-S.D.) is giving his senators broad leeway and tons of cash to preserve GOP control of the Senate. "I do see the Senate as a firewall in a lot of ways," Thune told Axios. "We will spend probably the next two years — if the House flips — trying to do impeachment or investigations, etc.," he said. Otherwise, the chamber will focus on judicial and executive nominations. Zoom out: Thune has three ways to help in the "tough environment" for Republicans in 2026. 🪧 1. Run against Washington: Thune said he understands if GOP candidates need to rhetorically distance themselves from Congress or even fellow Republicans in D.C., including himself. And when it comes to distancing from President Trump: "In some places the president's coming in, some places he isn't." Candidates can draw their own conclusions, Thune said. Republican candidates are increasingly concluding that to win their races, they need to break with Trump on some issues. 🗳️ 2. Vote for your state: Thune's policy with senators is " don't surprise us and when you can, stay with the team," but "do what's in the best interest of you and your state." That could lead to a rebuke of Trump when Democrats force another vote on an Iran war powers resolution, expected before the Senate breaks for October. People's views have "evolved and changed" as the war has dragged on, he said. Many senators are "responding to what they're hearing back home." "That's a really hard vote," Thune acknowledged. " Any time you are committing your country to putting young men and women in harm's way — those are the hardest votes you'll make." He hopes Republicans will stick together to win the vote. What to watch: Thune wants to give Republicans more votes before the break to champion back home. He sees an opportunity with permitting reform legislation, which is being negotiated behind the scenes. Thune said it's possible he sets up a procedural vote on it after the final vote on the Protect College Sports bill. Thune is also floating a vote on the House-passed legislation targeting data center energy costs if the Senate remains in town next week. 💰 3. Spend cash like crazy: The Thune-linked Senate Leadership Fund is set to spend nearly $280 million in video advertising this year — more than any other group, according to AdImpact. Texas PAC, which is affiliated with SLF, is on track to spend another $112 million. " Texas is expensive ," Thune said, but "we're doing everything we can to help. We can't afford to lose Texas." The bottom line: "That's ultimately up to the conference," Thune emphasized when asked if he'd run again if the GOP lost the majority, but "that's the plan." "The elections are going to be really important — I think – in how we view what happens next." Thune said you can't "rule anything in or out" when asked if he could face a challenger for the position. "But I think we worked really hard to create an environment here that is conducive to individual senators being able to achieve their objectives," he said. "I think, in this job, you have to be a good listener."

events.title: How the oil capital of the US welcomed a solar power boom
events.summary: Farmer Steve Cargil is now paid $200,000 a year for hosting a solar farm on his land Published 24 September 2026, 00:12 BST Steve Cargil's family has farmed the flat, dry land around Uvalde, a small city in southwest Texas, since 1953. Cargil, 67, had always assumed that one of his three children would eventually take it over, the way he had from his father. But that assumption took a hit one night in 2018 after a violent hailstorm. Cargil and his son, Ryan, had spent months nursing crops of cabbage and onions to harvest. Then a storm rolled through and destroyed them overnight. "I remember my son saying, 'Dad, I just don't know if I can do this. You do everything right, and we work so hard, and you come out one morning and it's all gone'," Cargil says. Cargil's farm was at risk of ending with him, he says, with none of his three children wanting to farm full time. For years, that left him wondering what would happen to the land, and to his own retirement, since farmers rarely have a pension to fall back on. Then in 2001 Cargil signed a deal to lease 600 acres of his land, about a quarter of the total, to a company called OCI Energy which built a vast solar farm. "Never in my wildest dreams did I think that a solar project would be on my farm," Cargil says. Looking back now, he calls it a blessing. The lease, which pays Cargil $200,000 (£150,000) a year, has let him keep his farm running through a punishing drought. He has been able to concentrate his water irrigation allowance on the land he still farms, and he has stopped losing sleep over rises in the price of things such as diesel and fertiliser. "It's changed my life." Texas, which remains the largest oil producer in the US, earlier this year overtook California to become the country's biggest generator of electricity from solar farms. , external And in March of last year, more electricity was produced by solar in Texas than from coal for the first time, according to the US Energy Information Administration. Solar farms can stretch out across the flat lands of Texas On hot afternoons, when demand for power peaks, solar is now regularly supplying around a third of the electricity used across Texas, says Mark Stover, executive director of the Texas Solar and Storage Association. He says that the solar boom is being driven by two main things. Firstly, it is cheap and quick to connect solar farms to Texas' power grid, which is separate to the rest of the US. Secondly, Texas has a huge and growing appetite for electricity, driven by a burgeoning population. Between 2015 and 2025, Texas's population increased by 15.8%, , external making it one of the fastest-growing states in the nation. "We need a whole lot of power in Texas, and we need it quickly," Stover says. Solar has also become inexpensive. James Scott, vice president of project development at OCI, says the technology has had years of small manufacturing gains that brought the price down to the point where it is now the cheapest way to generate power in the state. "No one would have believed that 20 years ago," Scott says. Once a project is built, he says, the price of the electricity it produces can be fixed for decades, since the fuel, sunlight, is free. "We'll charge you $40 a megawatt hour for the next 25 years," Scott says, adding that large buyers such as Amazon and Apple value being able to lock in a price for that long. By contrast, new coal plants in the US produce power at nearly $90 megawatts per hour, says the Energy Information Administration. Farmers have become central to that growth because solar developers need large stretches of flat land. Stover says the industry is now paying out multigenerational income to families through leases that typically run 25 to 30 years and rise in value each year, letting some retire, set up family trusts, or simply keep a farm solvent. Stover argues solar's footprint is smaller than critics assume. "The industry is utilizing less than 0.15% of Texas land," he says. Texas is now the largest producer of solar farm power in the US Yet solar has its opponents. In Franklin County, in northeast Texas, a small group of residents has spent the past few years fighting its growth. BF Hicks, a local lawyer whose family has owned land in the county since the 1800s, says he watched neighbours sign 30-year leases with solar companies and bulldozers clear centuries-old oak trees near his property. He describes a summer when smoke from burning cleared land hung over his town for weeks. "It got real personal," he says, when a solar farm was built next to his family's cemetery. His relatives have been buried here dating back two centuries. David Truesdale, a retired federal law enforcement agent who moved to the county to get away from city life, says he became involved after learning that a neighbouring solar project would sit near his home. And that under Texan law no environmental review was required.

events.title: £170 a bag? Protein users squeezed as prices soar
events.summary: The cost of the whey protein Amarpreet Singh buys has almost tripled since 2020 Published 24 September 2026, 00:12 BST Amarpreet Singh has been drinking protein shakes since he was 16. The 30-year-old, who lives in London and works in banking, started going to the gym at a time when he says protein supplements were mostly associated with bodybuilders. Fourteen years later, shakes are still part of his routine, but they have become considerably more expensive. He says a 4.5kg bag of the whey protein he buys cost around £60 in 2020. By last year, the price had gone up to £120, though he managed to get one from eBay for £90. Among his gym friends, the rising prices have even been given a nickname – "proteinflation". Student Evie says the tub she buys is quite expensive for the size of it Over the years, protein powders and shakes have attracted a much broader customer base, while food manufacturers now offer high-protein versions of everything from bagels to water. Evie Lewis is a more recent buyer of protein powder. The 19-year-old University of Manchester student began using it a few months ago because she felt she wasn't getting enough protein in her diet. "You hear a lot more about protein now on social media," she says. But at £32.99 for a 420g tub, she's feeling the high price and tries to make the product stretch. "I've been rationing it and using less than what's suggested," she admits. Max Longman, 32, from Manchester, works in real estate and has been taking protein supplements for 10 years, originally to help him gain weight. He now drinks a protein shake every day and says his monthly spending on whey protein has risen from around £45 a year ago to £60 now. "Loads of foods have protein added to them now. Up until a few years ago, I'd never heard of high-protein yoghurt, and now I eat it three or four times a week," he says. Max Longman has been taking protein supplements for 10 years More recently, weight-loss drugs such as Wegovy and Mounjaro have added another source of demand. People taking these drugs typically eat less, and are often encouraged to make sure they get enough protein while losing weight to help preserve muscle. But that growing appetite for protein is running up against a problem - supply has not kept pace. And the result has been a sharp rise in the wholesale price of some key ingredients, and consumers are feeling the squeeze. High whey protein prices take chunk out of THG profits Published 6 August 2025 Food firms scramble to meet the high-protein craze Published 7 October 2025 According to global market intelligence platform Expana, the European price of one widely used type of high-protein whey was 130% higher in late August than a year earlier, and more than four times its level three years ago. There is no equivalent UK measure, but Expana says the UK market is closely linked to mainland Europe, where some British businesses source their whey protein. Other dairy proteins have also become more expensive, with another type of whey protein up 60% over the year, while one type of milk protein concentrate was up 80%. Manufacturers say that increasing production takes time and is costly, as producing high-protein whey requires specialist processing and drying equipment. So some are starting to adapt what they make, by changing recipes or looking for cheaper sources of protein. Kieran Fisher's company Warrior is launching a product using cheaper sources of protein Warrior, a UK sports nutrition company, is one of those looking for alternatives. "Our whey protein powder was £12.50 on the shelf last year. We've put that up to £17.99 and we're still subsidising that from other aspects of the business," says its founder Kieran Fisher. The company is now launching a product using other sources of protein, which Fisher says costs around half as much as whey. The effects are also being felt outside the fitness market. Dairy proteins are used in infant formula, and Expana says higher dairy protein costs have contributed to price rises there too. There are, however, early signs that the market is starting to adjust. Wholesale prices for high-protein whey have begun to level off over the past couple of months, although they remain much higher than they were a few years ago. For now though, the higher prices aren't putting off Max. "It feels like protein is so important now, a lot more than it used to be. It's pushed out everywhere," he says. "If you're doing exercise and not taking any, you feel like you wouldn't be recovering properly." But for students like Evie, managing on a much tighter budget, it's a different story. "It was affordable on my gap year [when she was working], but now I'm at university, I don't think I'll continue buying it. It's not a necessity right now," she says. Amarpreet says he will continue buying protein, but admits "it's becoming a luxury". He says £170 for a bag is too much for him, so he's switching to a cheaper brand, which he can get for about £100 a bag.

events.title: US rejects pleas from OpenAI, Anthropic for global AI standards
events.summary: Sam Altman of OpenAI has become a key figure in the AI technology development. The heads of OpenAI, Anthropic, and Hugging Face have told the UN that the current pace of artificial intelligence (AI) development, and the risks it poses to society, demands international coordination. Altman called for common risk evaluation standards, as did Dario Amodei of Anthropic, a main rival of OpenAI, and Clement Delangue of Hugging Face. Earlier this month, Amodei wrote an essay welcomed by Altman and others calling an AI development slowdown in response to fears about the technology's threat to humanity. However, at the same UN conference, a key technology advisor to US President Donald Trump, rejected the idea any new form of AI regulation. Michael Kratsios, a former Scale AI executive, admitted that the speed of AI development is increasing and that there are risks presented by the technology, but told the UN this was not reason enough "to pause development or constrain it with new global governance structures". "International dialogue in this forum and others cannot be allowed to drift toward global governance," Kratsios added. Kratsios's comments echoed similar statements made by Trump in recent weeks. Trump told the UN on Tuesday he wanted to rebrand it "super intelligence" and has strongly opposed any idea of an AI slowdown because of the US's competitive advantage in the sector. "We're leading China on AI... and, frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins ," he said earlier this month. Sam Altman of OpenAI and other AI chief executives expressed a different view in their talks to the UN on Wednesday. "If AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone," said Altman. He told the UN that he wanted countries to start working together toward "the collective good in the face of powerful new technology". He called for "national and international" AI standards on measuring the capabilities of an AI tool, assessing related risks, AI safeguards, and the degree to which human oversight over such tools is maintained. He also called for "speedy incident reporting, classification, and reporting protocols so the world can learn from failures before they become catastrophes". "We need common standards so countries can compare evidence, verify compliance, and have a shared language and understanding what is happening," Altman added. Not all AI workers think the tech could kill everyone Published 4 days ago AI 'kill switch' may need to be mandatory, Anthropic co-founder tells BBC Published 15 September AI staff 'genuinely frightened' for humanity's future, ex-Anthropic researcher tells BBC Published 13 September Anthropic's Amodei and Hugging Face's Delangue made similar comments in their speeches. Amodei said that AI "if managed poorly... could be a risk to humanity as a whole". He added that further development of AI tools calls for "even more stringent standards of safety". "We will slow down as much as necessary in order to make sure that every successive AI technology that we release is actually safe," Amodei added. "But regardless of what we do, managing these risks is ultimately bigger than any one company, and it has an industry-wide and global scale." Hugging Face's Delangue said: "The global community needs stronger standards for monitoring and incident disclosure." All three of the executives are based in the US and directly involved in the development of AI technology. Hugging Face, a platform for AI developers, more recently rose to prominence after it admitted to being hacked by AI agents , or AI bots that operate somewhat autonomously, that came out of OpenAI. Hugging Face has since been acquired by AI chipmaker Nvidia. The Hugging Face hack has been treated as a 'wake-up call' within the industry for the ways in which AI technology has advanced and could hypothetically act in ways that could harm humanity. events.title: Susan Collins Dismissed Our Reporting as Old News. Some of Her Claims Aren’t True.
events.summary: Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, at the U.S. Capitol in August Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images As the scandal over Susan Collins’ relationship with Hawaii defense contractor Navatek became the central issue in her hotly contested senate campaign, she and her top aides mustered a defense with a series of incorrect and misleading claims. Read More The FBI Anti-Corruption Squad Was Circling Susan Collins — Until Trump Got in the Way On Tuesday, ProPublica published an investigation into the senior senator from Maine’s relationship with Martin Kao, the former Navatek CEO and a major donor who told law enforcement he exchanged campaign cash for government contracts. His confession came after his guilty plea for campaign finance and loan fraud. The ProPublica story revealed that the FBI had been circling the senator, her top aides and a pro-Collins super PAC in recent years, asking questions about their relationship with Navatek. Since returning to office, President Donald Trump fired or pushed out most of the federal agents and lawyers investigating high-profile federal corruption matters, including those working on the Kao case. The dismissals ended the corruption review, which was in its early stages. After the story published, Collins and her campaign denied any wrongdoing in numerous media appearances. Some of the statements made by Collins and her representatives are not accurate. Collins : “In 2021, the Biden Justice Department found there was no wrongdoing by anyone on my campaign staff, my office or me.” Collins : “The Biden-led Justice Department and FBI totally cleared my office, my campaign and me five years ago of these seven-year-old allegations.” An FBI spokesperson told ProPublica the agency had investigated claims against Collins years ago “and ultimately found nothing implicating Senator Collins or Senator Collins’ campaign.” But the investigation at the center of ProPublica’s story was based on claims Kao made between 2022 through 2024 — not seven years ago, as Collins states. That investigation did not conclude under President Joe Biden but under Trump, in 2025, after his administration purged the agents and Department of Justice attorneys assigned to the case. Collins is referring to the FBI’s initial investigation of Kao, which started in 2021. No one in Collins’ orbit was charged as a result of that earlier investigation.  FBI records reviewed by ProPublica show the agency remained interested in the conduct of Collins and her staff right up until the most recent phase of their investigation was shut down under Trump. The documents show that Kao was still answering agents’ questions as late as September 2024, when he sat for a two-day interview with FBI agents at the U.S. attorney’s office in Honolulu. During that interview, Kao provided them with a 50-page document offering many new allegations about his interactions with elected officials, including Collins. And in early 2025, FBI agents were still examining Kao’s relationship with Collins, her staffers and employees of the super PAC, ProPublica found. Annie Clark, deputy chief of staff to Collins : “The FBI and the Court obviously did not believe Kao.” The judge in Kao’s sentencing ultimately offered him no benefit for his cooperation with federal authorities, sentencing him to 87 months in federal prison. While Kao had credibility issues — as a convicted felon — FBI documents seen by ProPublica show that agents were able to corroborate some of his claims. “Pursuant to a Grand Jury Subpoena issued to Navatek, related to the previous investigation, hundreds of thousands of documents were provided to the FBI,” agents wrote in a December 2024 document. “Several emails and other documents corroborate Kao’s statements made to the FBI.” In addition, people familiar with the investigation told ProPublica that FBI agents found Kao to be credible. Clark : “ProPublica took the word of someone who pled guilty to five counts of money laundering, three counts of wire fraud, one count of bank fraud, and making false submissions to the FEC.” ProPublica did not simply take Kao at his word but reviewed a trove of evidence gathered by the FBI. It also examined thousands of pages of legal records and interviewed dozens of people familiar with Navatek, its Washington operations and the FBI inquiry to independently corroborate much of Kao’s account. For instance, Kao said that Scott Reed, the head of the Collins super PAC, promised to make the senator aware that Kao was the person behind a large, anonymous donation to the super PAC made through a shell company. We published emails between Reed and Kao showing that Kao told Reed the name of the shell company he was using to anonymize his $150,000 donation. And we included an email from someone working for Reed to a Navatek representative asking for Kao’s number so Collins could thank him for the donation. These are consistent with Kao’s version of events. Steve Abbott, Collins’ campaign manager, said at a Wednesday press conference, “We have no record of her calling him.” But he added that such a phone call would not be unusual: “We routinely thank people for contributions. … We try to thank everybody.” Reed did not answer detailed questions about the $150,000 donation but said he didn’t speak to Collins about Kao. He added, “I understand Martin Kao is now sitting in federal prison.” Do You Have Information About Political Dealmaking in Washington? We’re still reporting on pay-for-play arrangements between powerful companies and elected officials. William Turton I want to hear from you. Please feel free to send tips or story ideas. events.title: Anthropic says its biology lab has already found something big
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Disrupt ticket savings of up to $200 + 50% off a second ends Sept 25, 11:59 p.m. PT. REGISTER HERE. Last week, Anthropic confirmed that it was operating a wet biology lab in the Bay Area where it uses its AI models to run physical experiments. This week, the AI giant announced that this lab has already made what it believes is a big discovery: a new enzyme “system” that has certain “properties reminiscent of CRISPR,” as Anthropic describes it . CRISPR is a natural immune system used by bacteria to fight off viruses that has become a gene-editing technology widely used by researchers . Essentially, what Anthropic says it found is a previously unknown enzyme system hidden in the DNA of bacteriophages, which are viruses that infect and replicate within bacteria. Anthropic’s researchers say this system behaves similarly to CRISPR in that it can “perform operations like cutting, copying, and pasting DNA.” It will be up to the broader research community to validate how big, or new, this discovery actually is. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei acknowledges that the discovery was based on the work of others and that a team from Stanford previously discovered a system “that is in some ways similar to the one Claude found,” he wrote on X . But Amodei and Anthropic are not just emphasizing the discovery. They are touting it was found “mostly, though not entirely, by Claude,” the CEO wrote. On the one hand, that is astounding. This lab was only established this spring (though Anthropic declined to be more specific about how many months it has been open). A discovery in just a few short months would be speedy enough work, but the team said it actually only took Claude 21 hours of concerted effort. Claude searched through data using about 950 agents that burned through 210 million tokens. Still, the revelation that Anthropic has been conducting biology experiments comes right after AI CEOs, including Amodei , publicly admitted that models have become so capable, and so potentially dangerous, that the industry must slow down and develop safety-testing procedures. This after a couple of his employees publicly said earlier this month that there’s a risk AI could kill us all . Amodei himself has said one of the things he fears most is that AI could be used for bioterrorism. But he also believes AI will “cure most diseases in 5-10 years,” he wrote. So Anthropic has clearly decided the rewards are worth the risks. Given that, perhaps the biggest reveal in this news isn’t the discovery itself but that the biology lab hasn’t let Claude loose. The physical experiments were done by humans. “Our lab, located in the Bay Area, looks like a typical molecular biology lab. We do research that involves only the lower-levels of the biosafety risk level (BSL-1 and BSL-2) and we do not handle pathogens that can infect humans. All of the lab work is performed by human scientists.” It’s also true that AI-powered biological research is hardly unique to Anthropic. Researchers from Stanford just published a paper on the work they are doing with LLMs and CRISPR. Researchers at UC San Francisco used AI to design enzymes from scratch . Google launched its first AI-powered biology research tool, AlphaFold, back in 2020 . So AI has clearly arrived in biological research beyond the AI labs pursuing it themselves. Yet, Amodei hasn’t ruled out a fully automated biology lab in the future. “Eventually it may even be possible for Claude itself to safely perform the experiments by autonomously controlling lab equipment, with appropriate safeguards in place, but we aren’t doing that today,” he said. events.title: Trump greets Xi on tarmac in rare gesture
events.summary: President Trump welcomed Xi Jinping at Joint Base Andrews for the Chinese leader's state visit to Washington D.C. Wednesday evening. Why it matters: U.S. presidents typically receive visiting foreign leaders at the White House, making Trump's airport welcome an unusual diplomatic gesture. The latest: Trump met Xi at the foot of the stairs after the Chinese leader's jet landed at Joint Base Andrews, the U.S. military base 13 miles southeast of the White House in Maryland. Zoom out: It's much more common for U.S. presidents to greet visiting leaders at the White House. In February 2025, Trump welcomed Volodymyr Zelensky at the West Wing entrance to kick off the Ukrainian leader's tense visit. In April of this year, King Charles III was received at the White House's South Portico. The big picture: Presidents in recent decades have occasionally greeted visiting popes at D.C.-area airports, but airport welcomes for other foreign leaders have largely fallen out of use. President John F. Kennedy personally welcomed several foreign leaders at Washington-area airports in 1962, including Ivory Coast President Félix Houphouët-Boigny. More recently, President George W. Bush greeted Pope Benedict XVI at Andrews in 2008, and President Obama greeted Pope Francis there in 2015. What they're saying: "President Xi hosted President Trump in China for a historic summit this summer, and President Trump is reciprocating his hospitality by welcoming the Chinese delegation for a reciprocal visit this week," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly told Axios. "The President will forge relationships with anyone in order to advance our national interests and make good deals for the American people." The bottom line: Trump's tarmac greeting revived a presidential practice that has become uncommon outside visits by popes.
